4220: "Depreciate" has two meanings — one about value, and one about opinion. The first is by far the more common and important of the two.
Meaning 1: To decrease in value, or to cause something to decrease in value

When the subject loses value on its own (intransitive use):

Something depreciates when its worth goes down over time — because of age, wear and tear, market conditions, or simply because something newer and better has come along.

  • "New cars depreciate the moment you drive them off the lot."
  • "The company's shares depreciated sharply during the recession."
  • "A country's currency depreciates when its economy weakens."

When you deliberately reduce the recorded value of something (transitive use):

This is very common in business and accounting. When a company owns an expensive asset — a machine, a vehicle, office equipment, a building — it doesn't record the full purchase cost as a single expense right away. Instead, it depreciates the asset: it spreads that cost out over the number of years the asset is expected to be useful, reducing its recorded value by a portion each year.

  • "The company depreciated its delivery trucks over six years."
  • "You may be able to depreciate certain business equipment on your tax return."

Here's a concrete example to make this crystal clear: A bakery buys a large oven for $20,000, and it's expected to last 10 years. Rather than recording a $20,000 expense in Year 1, the bakery depreciates it — recording a $2,000 reduction each year. After Year 1, the oven's book value is $18,000. After Year 2, it's $16,000. And so on, until it reaches zero (or a small leftover value called "salvage value"). The act of doing this, year after year, is called "depreciating the asset."

The opposite of depreciate is appreciate:

To appreciate means to increase in value — the exact reverse. Real estate, rare art, and gold tend to appreciate over time, while cars, electronics, and most machinery tend to depreciate. Keeping this pair in mind makes both words easier to remember.

  • "While her car depreciated every year, her house appreciated steadily."
Meaning 2: To regard or portray something as less worthy than it really is — to belittle or undervalue

Less commonly, you can "depreciate" something (or someone) by treating it as insignificant, speaking of it dismissively, or portraying its worth as lower than it actually is.

  • "He constantly depreciated her contributions during team meetings."
  • "Don't depreciate the impact of small, consistent daily habits."

Important note: This second meaning is increasingly handled by a closely related word, "deprecate" (see below). In modern usage, many writers and speakers use "deprecate" for the "belittle or express disapproval" sense, and "depreciate" for the financial sense. You may encounter both in writing, particularly in older texts.
Depreciate vs. Deprecate — Don't Mix These Up

Because these words look almost identical, they cause a lot of confusion. Here is the clean distinction:

Depreciate → centers on value. Something loses its worth over time, or you reduce its recorded worth.

Deprecate → centers on disapproval. Someone expresses that they dislike, frown upon, or regard something as unworthy.

  • "The new phone model caused last year's version to depreciate in market value." (value fell)
  • "The organization deprecated the use of aggressive sales tactics." (expressed disapproval)

In software and technology, you will very often see the word "deprecated" — it means a feature, function, or method is no longer recommended and is being phased out. ("This command is deprecated; please switch to the updated version.")

You have almost certainly also heard the phrase "self-deprecating" — it means putting yourself down or making yourself seem smaller than you are, often in a humorous or modest way. ("His self-deprecating humor made him instantly likable.") This comes from deprecate, not depreciate — though historically the two overlapped.

• Depreciation (noun): the process of losing value, or the specific amount lost — "Annual depreciation on that van is $4,000."
  • Depreciated (past tense / adjective): "a heavily depreciated asset," "the currency has depreciated by 15%."
  • Depreciating (present participle): "a rapidly depreciating vehicle," "depreciating the equipment annually."
  • Depreciable (adjective): eligible to be officially depreciated for accounting or tax purposes — "Is this computer purchase depreciable?"
  • Depreciatory (adjective, rare): tending to depreciate or belittle — "depreciatory remarks."

"Depreciate" means to go down in value — whether it's a car aging in your driveway, a nation's currency weakening against others, or a business methodically writing down the cost of its equipment on its books. The second meaning — to belittle or undervalue something — is real but much less frequent in everyday language, and its role has largely been taken over by the word "deprecate" in modern usage.

If you remember just one thing: things that lose value over time depreciate, and things that gain value over time appreciate. That contrast alone will serve you well in almost every situation where this word comes up.
4221:
Depreciation means the loss in value of something over time. That "something" is typically a physical object or a currency. A brand-new car is worth more on the day you buy it than it will be a year later, and even less five years after that. That ongoing, gradual reduction in value — that is depreciation.

Now, that's the everyday intuition. But this word carries a great deal more meaning and precision, especially in the worlds of accounting, business, and economics.

This is the most important and widely used sense of the word, so we'll spend the most time here.

The Big Idea

When a company buys an expensive asset — say, a machine for $100,000 — it doesn't treat that as a $100,000 loss in the first year, even though it spent the money then. Why not? Because that machine will be put to work for many years into the future. It would be misleading and inaccurate to say "we lost $100,000 this year" when the machine will generate value for the next decade.

So instead, the company spreads that $100,000 cost across all the years it expects to use the machine. If the machine is expected to last 10 years, the company records a portion of the cost — say, $10,000 — as an expense each year. That yearly amount is the depreciation. In other words, accounting depreciation is the systematic, year-by-year recognition of an asset gradually being "used up."

This gives a far more truthful picture of a company's real costs and profits. It's also important for tax purposes: governments generally allow businesses to deduct depreciation as an expense, which reduces the amount of tax they owe.

What Can Be Depreciated?

Not everything qualifies. An asset must be a tangible (physical) asset that has a finite useful life — meaning it will eventually wear out, become outdated, or stop being useful. Common depreciable assets include machinery, vehicles, computers, equipment, and buildings.

There is one major exception: land does not depreciate. Land doesn't get worn out or used up. It just sits there, and so its cost is never spread out or reduced in the accounting books.

Intangible assets (things you can't physically touch, like patents or trademarks) go through a similar process, but that process has its own name — amortization, not depreciation. More on that distinction later.

Key Terms You Must Know

To truly understand depreciation, you need to know the handful of terms that orbit it.

Useful life is the estimated number of years a company expects to use an asset. A company car might have a useful life of five years. Heavy industrial machinery might have a useful life of twenty years. This is an estimate, and different companies (or tax authorities) may estimate differently for the same type of asset.

Salvage value (also called residual value) is the estimated value the asset will still have at the end of its useful life. For example, if a company plans to sell an old machine for scrap after ten years and expects to get $5,000 for it, that $5,000 is the salvage value. Some assets have a salvage value of zero.

Depreciable cost (also called depreciable base) is the total amount that will actually be depreciated — not the full purchase price, but the purchase price minus the salvage value. If a machine costs $100,000 and has a salvage value of $5,000, the depreciable cost is $95,000. That $95,000 is what gets spread over the asset's life.

Accumulated depreciation is the running total of all depreciation recorded for an asset since it was first purchased. If $10,000 is depreciated each year, then after three years, the accumulated depreciation is $30,000. This number grows every year until the asset is fully depreciated or disposed of.

Book value (also called carrying value or net book value) is the value at which an asset appears in the company's accounting records at any given moment. It is calculated simply as the original cost of the asset minus the accumulated depreciation. If the machine originally cost $100,000 and has accumulated depreciation of $40,000, its book value is $60,000. It's crucial to understand that book value is a purely accounting figure — it may or may not match what you could actually sell the asset for in the real world (the market value).

Methods of Depreciation

Not every asset loses value at the same rate, and different methods of calculating depreciation reflect different real-world patterns of value loss. The three most important methods are:

Straight-line depreciation is the simplest and most common method. The same fixed amount is depreciated every single year throughout the asset's life. The formula is: (Cost − Salvage value) ÷ Useful life = Annual depreciation. So for our machine: ($100,000 − $5,000) ÷ 10 years = $9,500 per year, every year for ten years. Think of it as a slow, steady, perfectly even decline — like a straight line going downward.

Declining balance depreciation is an accelerated method, meaning more depreciation is recorded in the early years and less in the later years. This makes sense for assets like cars and computers, which tend to lose the most value right after you buy them and then lose value more slowly as they age. A common version is the double declining balance method, where the annual depreciation rate is twice what it would be under the straight-line method. The result is front-loaded depreciation — you write off more of the cost early, less later.

Units of production depreciation ties depreciation directly to how much the asset is actually used, rather than to the passage of time. If a machine is expected to produce one million units over its lifetime, you calculate depreciation per unit produced, and then multiply by how many units were actually produced each year. In a year of heavy production, depreciation is high; in a quiet year, it's low. This is realistic for assets where physical wear depends directly on usage.

The choice of method genuinely matters — it affects how a company's profits appear on paper from year to year, even if the underlying economic reality is the same. For this reason, accounting standards and tax laws often specify or restrict which methods are permissible.

In economics, depreciation describes the decline in the value of one currency relative to another currency. If the British Pound weakens against the US Dollar — meaning you now need more Pounds to buy the same number of Dollars — the Pound is said to have depreciated against the Dollar.

Currency depreciation is typically caused by factors like high inflation within a country (when prices rise fast domestically, the currency tends to weaken internationally), low interest rates, a weak or slowing economy, an oversupply of the currency relative to demand, or political instability that erodes investor confidence.

One important distinction: currency depreciation usually refers to a decline in a currency's value that happens naturally in the open market, driven by supply and demand forces. When a government or central bank deliberately and officially reduces the value of its own currency by policy decision, that specific action is technically called devaluation, not depreciation — although in casual conversation, the two words are sometimes used interchangeably.

Outside of finance and economics, depreciation is occasionally used in a broader, more literary sense to mean any decline in value, importance, quality, or esteem. You might see phrases like "the depreciation of human effort" or "the depreciation of artistic standards," meaning those things are being undervalued or are declining in standing. This usage is less common, but you may encounter it in formal writing or older texts.
Important Distinctions: Words Easily Confused with Depreciation

Amortization is the same concept as accounting depreciation, but it applies to intangible assets — things that have no physical form, such as patents, copyrights, trademarks, or goodwill (the value of a business's reputation and customer base). If depreciation is for things you can touch, amortization is for things you cannot. In practice, people often use the word "amortization" in another context too — for the gradual repayment of a loan (like a mortgage), where each payment chips away at the principal balance over time.

Depletion is a similar concept but applies specifically to natural resources — oil reserves, coal deposits, timber forests, mineral mines. As the resource is extracted and used up, its recorded value is reduced through depletion. The more you take out of the ground, the more the asset depletes.

Obsolescence is a cause of depreciation but is not the same thing. Obsolescence means an asset has become outdated or no longer useful — often because better technology has replaced it. A machine can be perfectly functional physically but still depreciate rapidly because something far better now exists. Obsolescence is one of several reasons an asset loses value; depreciation is the measurement and recognition of that loss.

Appreciation is the direct opposite of depreciation. When something increases in value over time, it appreciates. Real estate and fine art, for example, often appreciate. Depreciation and appreciation are antonyms.

Depreciation, in its fullest sense, is the recognition that things lose value — and that this loss should be measured, recorded, and accounted for honestly. Whether it's a machine that physically wears out, a currency that weakens in global markets, or an asset that becomes obsolete, depreciation is the word that captures that downward journey in value.

In accounting, what makes the concept especially powerful is that it turns a one-time purchase into a cost that is spread intelligently across time, aligning the expense with the actual benefit received — which is the cornerstone of accurate, honest financial reporting.
4222:
Depredation means the act of causing serious damage, destruction, or loss — especially by attacking, plundering, or repeatedly harming something over time. Think of it as the harm left behind when something or someone strips away, destroys, or ravages what was once whole and valuable.

Depredation is about destructive taking or harming — not a small, accidental damage, but the kind of severe, often repeated destruction that leaves something significantly worse off than before.

Many words describe damage, but depredation carries a specific weight. It suggests that the destruction is:

  • Predatory in nature — it comes from something actively attacking or feeding on another.
  • Repeated or ongoing — not a single blow, but a pattern of harm inflicted over and over.
  • Serious and significant — not a scratch, but a ravaging.

This is why the word is almost always used in the plural form: "depredations." When you see "depredations," it signals a series of destructive acts, not just one isolated incident.

This is where the word becomes wonderfully flexible. Depredations can be committed by:

1. Humans — especially invaders, raiders, or criminals
This is the most classical use. Armies, pirates, bandits, or looters who attack, steal, and destroy are said to commit depredations. The word perfectly captures the brutal, repeated nature of such raids.

"The depredations of the invading army left village after village in ruins."

"The coastal towns lived in constant fear of the depredations of pirates."

2. Animals
When predators — wolves, foxes, rats, locusts — repeatedly attack livestock, crops, or ecosystems, their damage is called depredation.

"The farmers had no way to protect their sheep from the depredations of wolves."

"The depredations of locusts wiped out the entire harvest within days."

3. Abstract forces — time, neglect, disease, weather
This is perhaps the most poetic use. Even invisible, slow forces can commit depredations. Time erodes monuments. Disease ravages a body. Neglect destroys a building. The word gives these forces the feeling of an active, relentless attacker.

"The depredations of time had reduced the once-grand palace to rubble."

"Years of neglect and the depredations of damp had rotted the old library's shelves."

Depredation is a formal, serious word. You will not hear it in everyday casual conversation. It belongs in history books, literary writing, journalism about war or environmental destruction, and formal speeches. When a writer chooses this word, they are signalling gravity — this is not minor harm, it is serious ravaging.
How to Feel the Difference from Similar Words

Several words sit near depredation in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Plunder / pillage / loot — these focus on stealing during an attack. Depredation is broader: it includes destruction even when nothing is taken.
  • Damage — too neutral and mild. Depredation implies something predatory and severe.
  • Devastation — describes the result (how bad things are). Depredation describes the act (the attacking/harming process itself).
  • Ravaging — very close to depredation, but ravaging is more about total destruction in one sweep. Depredation more often implies repeated harm over time.

Here is the cleanest, most complete way to hold the meaning in your mind:

Depredation is the act of repeatedly and harmfully attacking, plundering, or destroying something — whether done by armies, animals, or even invisible forces like time and neglect.

When you see the word, picture something relentless — a wolf returning to the flock night after night, an army burning town after town, or centuries of wind and rain slowly devouring a stone monument. That relentless, destructive force is depredation.
A Few Final Sentences to Cement It

Read these slowly and let the meaning sink in:

  • "The region never fully recovered from the depredations of the decades-long civil war."
  • "Scientists are working to understand the depredations of the pine beetle on North American forests."
  • "Her journals describe, in painful detail, the depredations of illness on her father's mind."
  • "The museum's restoration team spent years reversing the depredations of a century of poor storage."

In every case, you feel the same thing: something valuable being worn down, attacked, or destroyed — not once, but relentlessly.
4223: "Depressed" describes something — a person, a place, or a surface — that is pushed down, lowered, or reduced below its normal, healthy, or expected level. That single idea of being brought low connects all of its uses.
Meaning 1: Emotional — Feeling Very Sad and Empty

This is the most common use. When a person is depressed, they feel a deep, heavy sadness that is much more serious than ordinary unhappiness. It is not just feeling bad for an hour because something went wrong. It is a persistent state where:

  • Everything feels hopeless and meaningless
  • They lose interest in things they used to enjoy
  • They feel tired, heavy, and unmotivated
  • They struggle to feel pleasure, joy, or excitement
  • The world feels grey and pointless

The key thing that separates "depressed" from just being "sad" is duration and depth. Sadness is a normal, passing emotion. Depression is a low, sunken state that lingers and colors everything.

She had been depressed for months after losing her job — she barely left her room and stopped talking to her friends.

You can also use it to describe a lighter, temporary version of this feeling in everyday speech:

I feel a bit depressed today — the weather is terrible and I have nothing to look forward to.

Here, the meaning is milder: just feeling low and gloomy. Context tells you how serious it is.

When used in a medical or psychological context, "depressed" means a person has clinical depression, which is a recognized mental health condition, not just a mood. A doctor might say a patient "is depressed" meaning they have been diagnosed with this illness.

Clinical depression involves the same emotional features described above, but they are present most of the time for at least two weeks or more, are severe enough to interfere with daily life, and are not simply caused by a specific life event like grief.

The psychiatrist confirmed that the patient was clinically depressed and needed treatment.

This use is more formal and precise than everyday emotional use.
Meaning 3: Economic — Reduced, Weakened, and Below Normal

When describing an economy, a market, a region, or a business, "depressed" means it is in a poor, weakened condition — with low activity, low prices, low employment, and little growth. Think of it as an economy that has been pushed down from where it should be.

The depressed housing market means that properties are selling for far less than their true value.

This was once a thriving industrial city, but it has become a depressed area with high unemployment and closed factories.

The imagery is the same — something that should be active and healthy has been brought low.
Meaning 4: Physical — Pushed Down or Sunken Below the Surrounding Surface

In a physical or technical sense, "depressed" means something has been pressed inward or sits lower than the area around it. It is used to describe surfaces, buttons, body parts, or structures.

The depressed key on the keyboard got stuck and would not spring back up.

The X-ray revealed a depressed fracture in the skull, where the bone had been pushed inward.

There was a depressed section in the road where the ground had sunk.

Again, the same idea: something that is lower than it should be, pushed in or sunken.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Sad — a normal, temporary emotional response to something specific. If your favorite team loses, you feel sad. It passes.

Unhappy — a broader dissatisfaction with life or a situation. Less intense than depressed.

Melancholy — a soft, reflective sadness, often with a somewhat poetic or thoughtful quality. You can be pleasantly melancholy. Depression is never pleasant.

Depressed — heavier, deeper, and more draining than all of the above. It implies that a person's energy, motivation, and sense of hope have been significantly reduced.

"Depressed" can range in severity depending on context:

  • Mildly depressed — just feeling a bit low or down
  • Deeply / severely depressed — in a serious psychological state that affects daily functioning
  • Chronically depressed — has been in this state for a long time

In economic use:

  • Slightly depressed — a market performing a bit below normal
  • Severely depressed — an economy in very poor, stagnant condition

No matter which meaning you encounter, the word always signals the same underlying idea: something has been brought lower than its normal, healthy, or expected state — whether that something is a person's spirit, an economy, or a physical surface. Once you hold onto that core image, every use of the word will make sense.
4224:
If something is depressing, it causes you to feel sad, hopeless, and emotionally heavy. It pulls your mood downward — not just for a second, but in a lingering way that makes things feel bleak, grey, or without hope.

Think of it this way: to depress something physically means to push it down. When something is emotionally depressing, it pushes your spirits and mood down.
What makes something "depressing"?

Almost anything can be depressing — a situation, a place, a piece of news, a film, a thought, even the weather:

  • "The documentary about climate change was deeply depressing."
  • "She lives in a depressing little room with no windows."
  • "It's depressing to think about how many years I've wasted."
  • "The statistics on child poverty are depressing."
  • "Three weeks of rain and no sunlight — so depressing."

Notice what these examples share: they all describe something that makes you feel a kind of emotional weight — a heaviness, a loss of hope, a gloomy sense that things are bad or difficult to change.
The emotional quality — what does it actually feel like?

When something is depressing, the feeling it creates is more than just sadness. It is:

  • Heavy — it weighs on you
  • Draining — it takes energy away from you
  • Hopeless — it can make things feel pointless or beyond fixing
  • Lingering — it doesn't go away quickly; it hangs over you

This is why people use depressing for things like grim statistics, a cheerless environment, or difficult realities — things that don't just make you briefly unhappy but make you feel down about life or the world for a while.
Depressing vs. similar words
These words are close in meaning but not the same:
Depressing vs. Sad:

Sad is an emotion you feel inside yourself. Depressing is a quality of the thing that causes that feeling.

  • ✅ "I felt sad." (describing your emotion)
  • ✅ "The film was depressing." (describing the film's effect on you)
  • ✅ "The depressing film made me feel sad."

You can also say "the film was sad," but depressing is stronger — it suggests a heavier, more hopeless feeling, not just sorrow.
Depressing vs. Disappointing:

Disappointing means something failed to meet your expectations. Depressing goes much further — it actively brings your mood down and makes you feel low or hopeless. A cancelled party is disappointing. A funeral in the rain is depressing.
Depressing vs. Gloomy:

Gloomy often describes an atmosphere or physical appearance (a dark, grey sky is gloomy). Depressing specifically describes the emotional effect on a person. A gloomy room can also be depressing if being in it makes you feel sad and hopeless — but depressing is always about what it does to your emotional state.
Depressing vs. Depressed — a critical difference

Many learners confuse these two. Here is the clear rule:

  • Depressing → describes the cause (the thing producing the feeling)
  • Depressed → describes the effect (the person feeling it)

"The news was depressing." — the news has this quality
"She felt depressed after hearing the news." — she has this feeling

You can link them together: "The depressing news left everyone feeling depressed."

You would never say "the news felt depressed" or "she felt depressing" — those are wrong.
How strong is it? Degrees of meaning

Depressing can be mild or severe, and you can signal this with adverbs:

  • Mild: "The traffic report was a bit depressing."
  • Moderate: "The working conditions there are pretty depressing."
  • Strong: "The whole situation was utterly / deeply / profoundly depressing."
Common patterns and phrases

• "It's depressing that..." — used to express hopelessness about a fact
    "It's depressing that so few people vote."
  • "How depressing!" — an exclamation of dismay
    "They closed the old bookshop? How depressing!"
  • "A depressing thought / reality / picture / sight"
    "The unemployment figures paint a depressing picture."
  • "Depressing news / statistics / results"
One final nuance — intentional vs. unintentional

When you call something depressing, you are not saying the person or thing intended to make you feel that way. A rainy day isn't trying to make you sad — but it can still be depressing. A well-meaning documentary about poverty isn't trying to hurt you — but it can still be depressing. The word is purely about the effect on your mood, not about intent.
In short:

Depressing describes anything that causes a heavy, sad, hopeless feeling — a feeling that lingers and drains you. It is stronger than sad and more emotional than disappointing. It describes the cause, not the person feeling it (that would be depressed).
4225:
Before diving into the different meanings, here is the one idea that runs through all of them:

Depression always means something has gone lower than its normal level — it has been pushed down, sunken in, or reduced.

That single idea is the key to understanding every use of this word. Once you have that, the rest falls into place.
Meaning 1: A feeling of deep sadness and low mood (everyday use)

In everyday language, depression refers to a heavy, persistent feeling of sadness, emptiness, and hopelessness. It is not ordinary sadness. Ordinary sadness is a natural emotional response — something bad happens, you feel sad, and eventually the feeling passes. Depression is heavier, darker, and does not lift easily on its own.

A person in depression typically feels:

  • Little or no joy, even in things they used to love
  • Low energy and motivation
  • A sense of heaviness, as if life has lost its colour
  • Hopelessness about the future

Example: "After her father died, she fell into a deep depression and withdrew from everyone."

People also use the word loosely for milder low moods: "This cold, grey weather is giving me depression." This is a casual, stretched use of the word — valid in conversation, but not clinically precise.
Meaning 2: A clinical mental health condition (medical use)

In medicine and psychology, depression — formally called major depressive disorder or clinical depression — is a recognised, diagnosable mental illness. This is not just feeling sad. It is a condition where the brain's chemistry and functioning are genuinely disrupted, making daily life very difficult.

For a doctor to diagnose clinical depression, the symptoms must be severe enough to interfere with a person's ability to work, maintain relationships, or function normally, and they must persist for at least two weeks.

The symptoms can include:

  • A persistently low or empty mood, lasting weeks or months
  • Loss of interest or pleasure in almost everything
  • Constant fatigue and physical slowing down
  • Difficulty thinking, concentrating, or making decisions
  • Disrupted sleep — either sleeping too much or too little
  • Changes in appetite and weight
  • Feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or self-blame
  • In severe cases, thoughts of death or suicide

Why this matters: Clinical depression is not a sign of weakness or a choice. It is a medical condition, just like diabetes or a broken bone, and it generally requires treatment — psychotherapy, medication, or both.

The main subtypes of clinical depression

Because "depression" is an umbrella term in medicine, doctors identify several specific forms:

Major depressive disorder — The most well-known form. The person experiences intense depressive episodes that significantly disrupt life. Episodes can last weeks or months.

Persistent depressive disorder (also called dysthymia) — A milder but chronic form of depression. The person does not feel as severely low as in major depression, but the low mood is present for most of the day, on most days, for at least two years. People with this condition often describe feeling "never quite okay" for a very long time.

Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) — Depression tied to the seasons. Most commonly, it begins in autumn or winter (when daylight hours shorten) and lifts in spring. It is thought to be linked to the brain's response to reduced sunlight.

Postpartum depression — Depression that occurs in a mother (and sometimes a father) after the birth of a child. It goes well beyond the typical "baby blues" — it is a serious condition that can make it very hard for the parent to care for the baby or themselves.

Bipolar depression — Some people have a condition called bipolar disorder, in which their mood cycles between extreme highs (mania or hypomania) and extreme lows. The depressive phase of this cycle is called bipolar depression. It is treated differently from other forms of depression, so identifying it correctly matters.

Psychotic depression — A severe form where clinical depression is accompanied by psychosis — hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there) or delusions (strongly held false beliefs).

Situational depression (adjustment disorder with depressed mood) — Depression triggered by a specific, identifiable life event, such as losing a job, going through a divorce, or surviving a disaster. It is considered a reaction to stress rather than a biological illness, though it can be just as painful.

In economics, a depression is a severe, prolonged collapse in economic activity. Think of the economy as something with a normal, healthy level of output. A recession is when it dips below that level for a while — bad, but not catastrophic. A depression is far worse: economic output falls sharply, unemployment surges to extremely high levels, businesses close in large numbers, people lose their savings, and the pain stretches on for years.

The most famous example in history is the Great Depression, which began with the crash of the U.S. stock market in 1929 and lasted through much of the 1930s. It caused unemployment rates of 25–30% in some countries and widespread poverty across the world.

The word fits perfectly here: just as a person in emotional depression is functioning far below their normal capacity, an economy in depression is performing far below what it should.
Meaning 4: A hollow or sunken area (physical/geographical)

In its most literal, concrete sense, depression simply means a dip, hollow, or sunken area in a surface — a place that is lower than everything around it.

Examples:

  • "There was a shallow depression in the earth where rainwater had collected."
  • "The geologist studied the depression formed by the ancient meteor impact."

In geography, a depression refers to an area of land that sits below sea level or below the surrounding terrain. The Dead Sea region is the most famous natural depression on Earth — it sits roughly 430 metres below sea level.

This is the most straightforward meaning of the word: no emotions, no economics — just a physical low point.
Meaning 5: A region of low atmospheric pressure (meteorology)

In weather science, a depression is a region where atmospheric pressure is lower than in the surrounding air. These regions are also called low-pressure systems or simply "lows." Air spirals inward and upward into a depression, which causes clouds to form and typically brings rain, strong winds, and unsettled weather.

Example: "A deep depression is moving in from the Atlantic, and heavy rainfall is expected across the region."

This is mainly a technical term you will encounter in weather forecasts and meteorology.
Meaning 6: An angle measured downward (mathematics and surveying)

In geometry and surveying, the angle of depression is the angle formed when you look downward from a horizontal line to an object below you. If you are standing on a cliff and looking down at a ship in the sea, the angle between your horizontal line of sight and the line pointing down to the ship is the angle of depression.

This is a precise, technical use of the word, most commonly found in trigonometry problems and surveying work.

Every single meaning of "depression" maps back to the same core idea — something pushed down or lowered:

  • Your mood has sunk below a healthy level → emotional depression
  • Your brain and body are functioning far below normal → clinical depression
  • The economy has collapsed below its normal activity → economic depression
  • A surface has a hollow point lower than the rest → physical depression
  • Atmospheric pressure is lower than surrounding air → meteorological depression
  • The angle goes downward from the horizontal → angle of depression

Understanding this single thread means you will never be confused by the word in any context.
The difference between being "sad" and having "depression"

This distinction is worth dwelling on because it matters enormously, especially in the medical sense.

Sadness is a normal, healthy human emotion. It comes in response to difficult events — grief, disappointment, failure. It is proportionate, temporary, and does not destroy your ability to function. Sadness is part of a full human life.

Depression (clinically) is different in three key ways:

  1. Persistence — it does not lift with time the way sadness does
  2. Pervasiveness — it colours everything, not just your reaction to one event
  3. Impairment — it interferes significantly with daily functioning

A person can be very sad without being depressed. And a person can be depressed without being able to point to any specific reason — the condition can arise even when life appears, from the outside, to be going well.
A note on how the word is used in conversation

You will hear "depression" used along a spectrum of seriousness:

  • Casually and loosely — "This Monday morning is giving me depression." (A light-hearted exaggeration of a low mood)
  • Seriously but informally — "He went into a deep depression after the breakup." (Describing a real, prolonged low — but not necessarily a clinical diagnosis)
  • Clinically and precisely — "She was diagnosed with major depression and started antidepressants." (A formal medical diagnosis)

Context usually makes clear which level of meaning is intended.
4226:
Deprivation means the condition of not having enough of something that you genuinely need — something whose absence causes you harm, suffering, or prevents you from living or functioning normally.

Think of it this way: there are things in life that aren't just "nice to have" but are actually necessary — sleep, food, love, freedom, clean water. When a person is cut off from these things, or simply doesn't have access to them, that state of going without is called deprivation.

The word carries two related ideas inside it:

  1. The act of being denied something — someone or something is blocking your access to what you need.
  2. The resulting condition of going without — the ongoing state of not having it.

Both meanings are valid, and in real usage, the word often captures both at the same time.
What Makes Deprivation Different from Just "Not Having Something"

Not having a luxury car is not deprivation. Not having food is.

The word specifically applies when the missing thing is something that a person needs for their health, development, dignity, or survival. It implies a sense of harm, suffering, or disadvantage caused by the absence. There's a built-in suggestion that the situation is serious and unfair or unfortunate — not just an ordinary gap or preference.

So deprivation is not a neutral word. It signals that something important is missing, and that the person is worse off because of it.

Deprivation can apply to almost any essential need. Here are the most common types:

Sleep deprivation — When a person doesn't get enough sleep over a sustained period. This is probably the most commonly used phrase with this word in everyday life. Sleep deprivation affects thinking, mood, and physical health.

Food deprivation / nutritional deprivation — Not having enough to eat, or not getting the right nutrients. This can lead to malnutrition and serious illness.

Emotional deprivation — Lacking love, warmth, affection, or emotional support — especially in childhood. Children who grow up without emotional connection can suffer lasting psychological harm.

Sensory deprivation — Being cut off from normal sensory input — light, sound, touch. This is used in psychology and also in torture contexts, because isolating the senses causes severe mental distress.

Social deprivation — Lacking meaningful human contact and community. Prisoners kept in isolation experience social deprivation. Elderly people who live completely alone can too.

Economic deprivation — Not having access to basic material needs — money, housing, clean water, healthcare. This is closely related to poverty.

Oxygen deprivation — Not getting enough oxygen to the brain or body, which can cause brain damage or death. This is used in medical contexts.

Cultural deprivation — Being denied access to education, cultural enrichment, or the tools needed to participate fully in society.

Deprivation exists on a spectrum.

On the milder end: a student pulling several all-nighters before exams experiences sleep deprivation. It's real, it causes real problems, but it's temporary and recoverable.

On the severe end: a child growing up in extreme poverty, without food, warmth, education, or love, experiences deprivation across multiple areas simultaneously. This kind of deep, sustained deprivation can shape an entire life and cause permanent damage.

The word fits both ends of the scale, though it carries a heavier emotional weight when the deprivation is severe or long-lasting.

There's an important idea called relative deprivation. This is when a person feels deprived not because they are objectively missing something essential, but because they have significantly less than the people around them.

For example, in a very wealthy neighborhood, a family that can't afford a car or vacations might feel a strong sense of deprivation — even though by global standards, their basic needs are met. The feeling of being deprived is real because humans naturally compare themselves to their immediate surroundings.

This concept is widely used in sociology and psychology to explain social tension, resentment, and unhappiness in unequal societies.

Here are example sentences showing the word in natural use:

  • Years of sleep deprivation had taken a visible toll on her health.
  • The report highlighted widespread deprivation in rural communities, where access to clean water remained unreliable.
  • Children who experience emotional deprivation in early life often struggle to form healthy relationships as adults.
  • The soldiers were subjected to sensory deprivation as part of an interrogation technique.
  • Economic deprivation and lack of education create a cycle that is very difficult to escape.
  • The study linked urban deprivation to higher rates of mental illness.

Certain words appear alongside "deprivation" so frequently that they form natural pairings:

  • Sleep deprivation — by far the most common collocation
  • Suffer deprivation — to endure the state of going without
  • Areas of deprivation — regions where poverty and lack of resources are widespread
  • Social deprivation
  • Relative deprivation
  • Sensory deprivation
  • Emotional deprivation
  • Deprivation of rights / liberty — used in legal and political language to mean the removal of someone's rights or freedoms

Since you'll encounter these related forms:

  • Deprive (verb) — to take something away from someone, or to deny them access to it. "Lack of sunlight deprives the body of Vitamin D." / "They were deprived of their freedom."
  • Deprived (adjective) — describes a person or place that lacks essential things. "She grew up in a deprived neighborhood." / "Deprived children often need extra support in school."
  • Deprivation (noun) — the state or condition itself. This is the form you asked about.
How Deprivation Differs from Similar Words

Lack is broader and more neutral. You can lack something trivial. Deprivation implies the missing thing is necessary and the absence is harmful.

Poverty refers specifically to material and financial shortage. Deprivation is wider — it includes emotional, social, and psychological needs too. All poverty involves deprivation, but not all deprivation involves poverty.

Shortage refers to an insufficient supply of something — usually for a group or society. Deprivation is more personal; it focuses on the person experiencing the absence and the harm it causes them.

Absence simply means something isn't there. It's completely neutral. Deprivation carries weight — it means the absence is causing damage.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

One last important point: deprivation is not a casual word. When you use it, you are signaling that the situation is serious. Writers, researchers, and journalists use it deliberately to highlight suffering, injustice, or urgent need. If you say someone "lacks sleep," it sounds mild. If you say someone experiences "sleep deprivation," it sounds medical and serious. If you say a community lives in "deprivation," you are painting a picture of sustained hardship.

This makes deprivation a powerful word — use it when the situation genuinely deserves that weight.
4227:
To deprive someone means to take away something from them that they need, deserve, or already have — leaving them without it.

The word always carries a sense of loss. The person being deprived ends up lacking something important or valuable. That "something" could be physical (food, sleep), abstract (freedom, opportunity), or anything in between.

Deprive almost always follows one grammatical pattern:

deprive + [person] + of + [thing]

Examples:

  • The noise deprived her of sleep.
  • The accident deprived him of his ability to walk.
  • Poverty deprived the children of a proper education.
  • The dictator deprived the citizens of their basic rights.

This "of" is essential. You deprive someone of something — not from something. Getting this right is important.

Not every kind of "not having something" counts as being deprived. The word carries a specific weight:

1. What's taken away matters.
You wouldn't say someone was deprived of a minor luxury unless you're being dramatic. Deprive is used when the thing taken away is genuinely important — sleep, rights, food, love, opportunity, freedom, dignity.

2. There is a sense of wrongness or harm.
Being deprived isn't neutral. It implies the person should have had that thing — by right, by need, or because they already possessed it. There's a suggestion of injustice or damage, even if no one is directly at fault.

3. The cause can be a person, a situation, or a circumstance.

  • A person can deprive another: The prison guard deprived the inmates of exercise.
  • A situation can deprive someone: The war deprived millions of their homes.
  • An illness can deprive someone: The disease slowly deprived her of her memory.

So deprive doesn't always mean someone is being cruel on purpose — sometimes life, illness, or circumstances do the depriving.

Deprive covers both:

  • Intentional: He deliberately deprived his employees of fair wages.
  • Unintentional: The long journey deprived the travellers of rest.

Context tells you which is which. The word itself doesn't commit to either.
Deprive in Different Areas of Life

Sleep: One of the most common uses.
Working night shifts deprived her of healthy sleep for years.

Rights and freedom:
The law deprived certain groups of their voting rights.

Emotional and social needs:
Growing up without affection deprived him of the confidence he needed.

Physical needs:
Extreme diets can deprive your body of essential nutrients.

Opportunity:
Being born in poverty deprived many talented students of higher education.

When you describe a person or a place as deprived, it means they lack the basic things needed for a decent life — usually due to poverty, inequality, or neglect.

  • He grew up in a deprived neighbourhood with poor schools and no green spaces.
  • Deprived children often face greater challenges in adult life.

Notice here that "deprived" works as an adjective describing a state of ongoing lack, not a single moment of taking away.

Deprivation is the condition of being deprived — the state of lacking something essential.

  • Sleep deprivation affects your memory and mood.
  • Sensory deprivation (blocking sight, sound, and touch) can cause hallucinations.
  • Economic deprivation leads to worse health outcomes.
How Deprive Differs from Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but not identical:

Deny — to refuse to give something, often in response to a request.
The bank denied him a loan. (He asked; they said no.)
Deprive is broader — the thing is taken away or withheld even if the person never formally asked.

Withhold — to deliberately hold something back, often something the person expects or is owed.
She withheld the information from him.
Withhold implies keeping something back quietly. Deprive implies the person ends up lacking something consequential.

Strip — to forcefully and completely remove something, often dignity, rank, or rights.
He was stripped of his title.
Strip feels more violent or sudden. Deprive can be gradual.

Rob — to take something by force or theft.
The illness robbed her of her hearing.
Rob is sometimes used figuratively like deprive, but it feels more sudden and aggressive.

So deprive sits in the middle — it's broader than withhold, less violent than rob or strip, and more consequential than deny.

To give you the full picture, here are words that mean the opposite of deprive:

  • Provide — to give someone what they need
  • Grant — to officially give or allow
  • Furnish — to supply with what is needed
  • Bestow — to give something as a gift or honour
  • Endow — to provide with a quality or resource

To deprive = to take away (or keep away) something important from someone, leaving them without something they need, deserve, or had a right to.

It's always followed by "of": deprive someone of something.
It implies harm, loss, and a sense that things are not as they should be.
It can describe a deliberate act or the effect of a situation, illness, or circumstance.

That is the complete picture of the word deprive — its meaning, its structure, its range, its forms, and how it compares to similar words. You now have everything you need.
4228: When we say someone or something is deprived, we mean they are seriously lacking things that people normally need or deserve in order to live a decent, healthy life. These are not small luxuries or wants — they are things most people would consider basic or essential: food, shelter, money, education, love, safety, opportunities, or basic rights.

The most important thing to understand about deprived is that it is not just about being without something. It carries two deeper ideas baked into it:

1. The lack causes real harm.
Being deprived isn't a minor inconvenience. It means going without something to the point where it damages a person's life, development, health, or well-being. A child who doesn't get a birthday cake is not deprived. A child who doesn't get enough food, love, or education is deprived.

2. The lack is unfair — something is being withheld or has been denied.
There is a quiet sense of injustice in the word. The person didn't choose this condition. It was done to them — by circumstances, by society, by poverty, by neglect, or by another person. They should have had these things, but they didn't get them.

This is why deprived carries weight and emotional gravity that a word like "lacking" does not.
What Can Someone Be Deprived Of?

This is a wide word. A person can be deprived of:

  • Material things — food, clean water, proper housing, clothing, money
  • Opportunities — education, healthcare, a fair chance in life
  • Emotional/social needs — love, affection, a stable family, human connection
  • Rights and freedoms — justice, safety, political rights
  • Physical needs — sleep, sunlight, rest, medical care

No matter which of these is missing, the word deprived fits if the lack is serious and harmful.

A person:
"She grew up deprived, without proper food or schooling."
Here it describes someone's overall condition in life.

A childhood, background, or upbringing:
"He had a deprived childhood." — This means his early years lacked the basic things a child needs: stability, care, education, safety.

A community, neighborhood, or area:
"This is one of the most deprived areas in the country." — This is very common usage. It describes a place where the people systematically lack economic resources, good schools, healthcare, and opportunities. This usage is standard in social, political, and news contexts.

Used in compound adjectives:
You will also see deprived attached to a specific thing being lacked, like:

  • sleep-deprived — a person who has not gotten enough sleep (this is the most common everyday use where the deprivation is more short-term)
  • emotionally deprived — a person who did not receive enough love, care, or emotional support
  • oxygen-deprived — lacking sufficient oxygen (used in medical contexts)

Deprived is not a neutral word. When you use it, you signal:

  • Sympathy and concern — You are acknowledging that someone has suffered or been treated unfairly.
  • Systemic or chronic suffering — Especially when talking about communities or childhoods, it implies this wasn't a one-time problem. It was an ongoing condition.
  • Something owed but not given — There is a moral dimension. The deprived person deserved what they didn't get.

Because of this weight, the word is often used in journalism, social policy, charity, and serious discussion. It's not casual.

• "Children from deprived backgrounds often struggle in school, not because they lack intelligence, but because they lack resources."
  • "The report highlighted several deprived communities where unemployment and poor housing had been problems for decades."
  • "After staying awake for two days, she was severely sleep-deprived and couldn't think clearly."
  • "He had been emotionally deprived as a child — his parents were rarely home and never expressed affection."
  • "Aid organizations are working to help deprived populations gain access to clean water."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Deprived vs. Poor:
Poor refers specifically to lacking money. Deprived is broader — it can include emotional, educational, and social lacks, not just financial ones. A wealthy person can be emotionally deprived.

Deprived vs. Underprivileged:
Both are often used interchangeably in social contexts. But underprivileged focuses on the absence of advantages and privileges that others enjoy (education, connections, comfort). Deprived is slightly stronger — it focuses on the absence of things that are genuinely necessary, not just advantageous.

Deprived vs. Disadvantaged:
Disadvantaged is a softer, more formal word often used in educational or policy language. It means placed at a disadvantage compared to others. Deprived is more emotionally direct and implies greater hardship.

Deprived vs. Neglected:
Neglected implies someone had a duty of care and failed to provide it (a neglected child). Deprived is broader — the cause doesn't have to be someone's personal failure; it can be poverty, war, or circumstance.

Deprived isn't all-or-nothing. You can be:

  • mildly deprived — lacking some important things but not in crisis
  • severely deprived — lacking even the most basic necessities for survival and dignity

And the word can be used comparatively: "This neighborhood is more deprived than the one across the river."

Deprived describes a person, place, childhood, or condition that has been denied or has gone seriously without the basic things — material, emotional, or social — that people need and deserve, often causing real and lasting harm.
4229:
Depth means how far something extends going inward, downward, or backward — away from the surface or the front. It is the measurement or quality of that inward distance.

Think of a swimming pool. The depth of that pool is the distance from the water's surface all the way down to the floor. That is depth in its purest, most physical sense.

The word "depth" lives in two worlds: the physical (literal) and the abstract (figurative). Once you understand the core idea — how far something extends inward — you will see how both worlds make perfect sense.

This is the most straightforward use. It refers to a measurable distance going in one of these directions:

  • Downward — from top to bottom: "The depth of the well is 40 feet."
  • Inward — from the opening to the back: "The depth of the cave is about 200 metres."
  • Backward — from the front edge to the rear: "The shelf has a depth of 30 cm."

Notice the pattern: depth always starts at a visible surface or edge and measures how far something goes away from you, into or below.

A wound can have depth (how deep the cut goes). A cupboard has depth (how far back it goes). A lake has depth (how far down the water reaches).

Here, depth no longer means a physical distance. Instead, it means how much substance, complexity, or detail something has — as opposed to being shallow or superficial.

Think of it this way: a shallow pool of water is easy to see the bottom of. A deep pool hides much more beneath the surface. We use this same image for ideas, knowledge, and thinking.

Knowledge and understanding:

  • "She has great depth of knowledge about history."
    → She knows a lot — not just the basic facts, but the nuances, the connections, the hidden details.

Writing, art, or ideas:

  • "This novel has real depth."
    → It is complex, layered, and meaningful — not simple or one-dimensional.

A person's character:

  • "He is a man of depth."
    → He thinks carefully, feels genuinely, and is not just focused on surface-level things.

The opposite of this kind of depth is shallowness — knowing only the surface of things, or being trivial and unreflective.
3. Emotional Depth — The Intensity of Feelings

When depth is used for emotions, it refers to how strong, sincere, or profound a feeling is.

  • "No one could doubt the depth of her love for her children."
    → Her love was not casual or lukewarm — it ran deep, like water that goes far below the surface.
  • "The depth of his sorrow was difficult to describe."
    → His sadness was not mild — it was intense, all-consuming, profound.

Again, the same logic applies: a deep feeling is one that goes far beneath the surface, beyond what is immediately visible.

You will sometimes encounter "depth" used to describe sensory qualities:

Colour:

  • "The depth of colour in this painting is remarkable."
    → The colours are rich, full, and layered — not flat or washed out. A "deep red" is a rich, dark red with intensity to it.

Sound/Voice:

  • "His voice had a wonderful depth."
    → His voice was low, resonant, and full — not thin or high-pitched. A "deep" voice carries weight and richness.
5. Depth in Teams, Resources, and Defence

In practical contexts — sports, the military, business — depth refers to having enough backup resources or layers beyond the first.

  • "The team lacks depth in its batting lineup."
    → If the top batsmen fail, there are not enough strong players further down the order.
  • "The army had strategic depth."
    → Even if the front lines were breached, there were more layers of defence behind.

The idea is the same: you are measuring not how far something goes physically, but how many layers of strength or resources exist beneath the obvious surface level.

When used in the plural — the depths — it means the deepest, most extreme, or most hidden part of something.

  • "The depths of the ocean" → the very bottom, the most remote and hidden part of the sea.
  • "The depths of winter" → the coldest, harshest point of winter — not its beginning or end, but its most extreme core.
  • "He sank to the depths of despair" → he reached the most extreme, lowest point of sadness imaginable.

The depths are always the innermost, most extreme version of something — the furthest from the surface.

"In depth" — means thoroughly, in great detail, not superficially.

  • "We studied the topic in depth." → We went beyond the surface and examined it carefully and completely.
  • "An in-depth analysis" → A thorough, detailed analysis.

"Out of one's depth" — means being in a situation that is too difficult for you to handle, like being in water deeper than you can stand in.

  • "When the conversation turned to advanced physics, she felt completely out of her depth."
    → She could not follow or contribute — the level was too far beyond her.

"Hidden depths" — used for a person who seems simple or plain at first but turns out to be far more complex, talented, or interesting than expected.

  • "She seems quiet, but she has hidden depths."
    → Beneath the surface, there is much more to her than you initially saw.

The remarkable thing about "depth" is that every single use of it traces back to the same image: measuring how far something goes below or beyond the surface.

Whether it is a physical well, a person's character, a piece of music, a team's strength, or a feeling — depth always asks: how far does this go beneath what I can immediately see?

Shallow things stay at the surface. Deep things go further — they have more to offer, more to explore, more layers hidden within. That is the soul of the word.
